title: Provider integration via declarative descriptor registry
context: Non-Claude agents were handled by five hardcoded provider switches; Codex/Gemini were stubbed with unknown cost. We wanted opt-in extensibility for more CLIs, including classifying local Ollama-backed models as $0.
decision: A new `provider` package loads embedded + user YAML descriptors that declare exe names, config dir, session glob, and token/model/cost field-paths. Session dispatch moved OUT of the `parser` package into the registry to break an import cycle. Enable-state is injected via an `EnabledFunc` seam (a DB-backed Settings UI is a follow-up, Plan 2). IDE-embedded providers are deferred to `source: custom:<id>` Go adapters.
consequences: Adding a JSONL-based provider is now a YAML change, no Go code. Non-Claude cost is now real or $0 (local) instead of always unknown. The `parser` package is no longer provider-aware.

title: Anthropic Messages API spawner as out-of-process SDK binary
context: The server had no way to run stage agents against the Anthropic API (only the claude CLI subprocess + OpenAI-compat/Ollama HTTP). The anthropic-sdk-go dependency would bloat server/go.mod and transitively affect all consumers.
decision: A standalone binary under plugins/anthropic-spawner (own go.mod, built GOWORK=off) invoked via the existing custom-exec adapter contract, surfaced as adapter_type 'anthropic'. A new LLMSpawnArgs.Stream flag disambiguates Spawn (false) vs SpawnStream (true). The binary reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from its inherited environment; the server locates it via DASHBOARD_ANTHROPIC_SPAWNER_CMD or PATH lookup of 'anthropic-spawner'.
consequences: anthropic-sdk-go stays out of server/go.mod. Adding the adapter required ~1 struct field (LLMSpawnArgs.Stream), 1 factory case (adapter_factory.go), a path resolver (anthropic_path.go), and the plugin binary. New out-of-process spawners follow the same pattern.

title: Shutdown releases streaming requests after a grace window, not immediately
context: http.Server.Shutdown waits for active non-hijacked connections but never cancels their request contexts. Every SSE handler selects only on r.Context().Done(), so with the SPA connected Shutdown always ran into the full shutdown.timeoutSeconds and returned context deadline exceeded — the desktop shell, the CLI's Ctrl-C path and POST /api/admin/restart all hung for 10s. Pointing BaseContext straight at the run context fixed the hang but cancelled every request the instant shutdown began, tearing in-flight mutations apart: tasks/handler.go passes r.Context() into orchestrator.ProgressTask, leaving a stage_run at running with pid=NULL that no sweep case reaps, plus the same shape in checkpoint/git.go, services/worktree_manager.go and api/agents/tmux.go.
decision: BaseContext returns a context built with context.WithoutCancel(ctx), so nothing but the server cancels it, and a time.AfterFunc cancels it RequestGraceDefault (2s) after shutdown starts. Ordinary in-flight requests finish inside the grace window; the long-lived streams are released after it and Shutdown returns well inside its own deadline. The grace is clamped to shutdownTimeout/2 when the configurable shutdown.timeoutSeconds is set below it. Alternatives rejected: RegisterOnShutdown plus a draining channel observed by each SSE loop, and a middleware applied only to stream routes — both work, but both require every future stream handler or route to opt in, and forgetting silently reintroduces the hang.
consequences: No per-handler opt-in and no route registration to maintain; a new streaming endpoint is covered automatically. Quit costs the grace window (~2s) rather than being instant. Hijacked terminal WebSocket read pumps also unblock on shutdown, which they did not before. Three timeouts now govern the shutdown lifecycle — api.ShutdownTimeout, the shutdown.timeoutSeconds setting, and desktop's drainTimeout backstop — and the ordering constraint between them (grace < shutdown timeout < desktop bound) is enforced only by clampRequestGrace and a comment.

title: Drive agents over ACP from a Go client, keeping the protocol on the spawn side
context: The dashboard reads an agent's intent by scraping a rendered terminal: ~1,275 lines across the pty host, screen emulation and AskUserQuestion parsing. The Agent Client Protocol standardises that channel and ~39 agents implement it, Gemini/Cursor/Copilot/Junie natively, Claude and Codex via adapters. A rewrite to TypeScript was evaluated because the Claude Agent SDK (canUseTool, elicitation) exists only for TS and Python. It was rejected: ACP itself has Go coverage, the TS advantage consists of exactly the features ACP is standardising, and the planned fleet requirement (agents on 1-n of the operator's own servers, own keys) makes a single static binary per node decisive, while a TS agent host would put Node on every server. Kotlin and Rust have an ACP SDK but no Agent SDK, so they gain nothing. provider.Adapter was considered as the integration point and rejected: it reads sessions off disk for IDE-embedded providers, whereas ACP is a process we start and talk to.
decision: Stay Go. Implement the client half of ACP in server/internal/acp and integrate on the spawn side via buildExecCommand, not through provider.Adapter. Depend on github.com/coder/acp-go-sdk replaced onto our fork github.com/lx-wnk/acp-go-sdk, with the replace confined to server/go.mod so the published sdk module is unaffected. Keep any Agent-SDK-dependent capability as an optional, local-only sidecar; fleet nodes run the plain CLI path with no Node. Treat ACP elicitation as out of scope: claude -p does not expose AskUserQuestion, so the existing pty path stays.
consequences: The parser, cost and roster paths need no change, because the ACP adapter writes the ordinary session JSONL with the ACP session id as the filename. Permissions arrive as a structured request instead of a screen scrape, and the gate is fail-closed by construction. In exchange we own a fork of the SDK, whose 87% generated surface makes a protocol bump a generator run plus fixes in ~1,451 handwritten lines; ACP v2 is in alpha and a migration is coming. If Anthropic ships native ACP in the CLI, the agent-side work becomes unnecessary and the client-side work becomes more valuable, so the client stays thin.
